'''Bernard Michael Haisch''' (23 August 1949 – 3 September 2026) was a German-born American [[astrophysics|astrophysicist]]<ref name="AMWS">{{cite encyclopedia |url=https://archive.org/details/americanmenwomen0008unse_j8x0/page/520/mode/2up?q=Haisch |title=American Men & Women of Science |publisher=Gale |year=2008 |editor-last=Henderson |editor-first=Andrea Kovacs |volume=7 |page=520 |entry=Bernard Michael Haisch}}</ref> who researched solar-stellar astrophysics, [[quantum electrodynamics]] (QED), observational X-ray and ultraviolet astronomy,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bernard Haisch publications |url=http://www.calphysics.org/haisch/publications.html |access-date=2025-10-30 |website=www.calphysics.org}}</ref> and [[stochastic electrodynamics]].<ref name="ufoskeptic">{{cite web|author=Haisch, Bernard|title=Dear Colleagues|website=ufoskeptic.org|url=https://www.ufoskeptic.org/home/}}</ref> Haisch, with Alfonso Rueda, developed a quantum [[vacuum]] inertia hypothesis proposing that the electromagnetic [[Quantum vacuum state|zero-point field]] contributes to [[inertial mass]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rueda|first1=Alfonso|last2=Haisch|first2=Bernard|title=Gravity and the quantum vacuum inertia hypothesis|journal=Annalen der Physik|volume=14|issue=8|pages=479–498|year=2005|doi=10.1002/andp.200510147|arxiv=gr-qc/0504061}}</ref> 

In 2002, Haisch became Chief Science Officer of ManyOne Networks. Since 2004, he has served as president of the Digital Universe Foundation, which aimed to create a peer-reviewed online encyclopedia as an alternative to Wikipedia. In 2006, Haisch published ''The God Theory: Universes, Zero-Point Fields and What's Behind It All'',<ref>{{cite book|last=Haisch|first=Bernard|title=The God Theory|publisher=Red Wheel/Weiser|year=2006|isbn=978-1-57863-374-6}}</ref> proposing that consciousness creates matter rather than vice versa, and that discoveries in quantum physics point to an underlying intelligence in the universe. Haisch attributed his spiritual interests to his studies at the [[Latin School of Indianapolis]] and the [[Saint Meinrad Seminary and School of Theology]].

== Life and career ==
Haisch was born in [[Stuttgart]], [[Württemberg-Baden]], [[West Germany]], on August 23, 1949; he spent a year in a [[minor seminary]]<ref name="Beyond">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DWaNAAAAQBAJ&dq=%22bernard+Haisch%22&pg=PA255|title=Beyond Atheism, Beyond God|first=Philip A.|last=Stahl|date=August 5, 2013|publisher=iUniverse|via=Google Books|page=155 |isbn=978-1-4759-9824-5 }}</ref> and earned a Ph.D. in [[astronomy]] from the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] in 1975. He then spent three years as a postdoctoral fellow at the [[Joint Institute for Laboratory Astrophysics]] at the [[University of Colorado at Boulder]].{{Citation needed|date=October 2025}}

He worked at the Solar & Astrophysics Laboratory at [[Lockheed Martin]] in [[Palo Alto, California]] and as deputy director of the Center for Extreme Ultraviolet Astrophysics Laboratory at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name="Martin">{{cite book |last=Martin |first=Stephan |title=Cosmic Conversations: Dialogues on the Nature of the Universe and the Search for Reality |publisher=Hampton Roads Publishing |year=2010 |page=49 |isbn=978-1-60163-077-3 |url=https://archive.org/details/cosmicconversati0000mart/page/48/mode/2up?q=%22Bernard+Haisch%22 }}</ref> 

In 1999, Haisch founded the California Institute for Physics and Astrophysics in [[Palo Alto, California]], an organization mainly devoted to studying the electromagnetic quantum vacuum and funded by private philanthropic money. The institute formerly employed five full-time physicists researching [[string theory]], [[general relativity]] and [[stochastic electrodynamics]]. Haisch served as the institute's director from 1999 until 2002.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.calphysics.org|title=Calphysics Institute|access-date=2025-10-18}}</ref>

In 2002, Haisch became the Chief Science Officer of ManyOne Networks.<ref name="Foreword" /> From 2004, he also served as president of the now-defunct [[Digital Universe Foundation]],<ref name="Foreword" /> which aimed to create a peer-reviewed alternative to [[English Wikipedia]].<ref name="Keim_2007">{{cite journal|author=Keim, Brandon|date=March 2007|title=News feature: WikiMedia|journal=[[Nature Medicine]]|publisher=Nature Publishing Group|volume=13|issue=3 |pages=231–233 |doi=10.1038/nm0307-231 |pmid=17342106 }}</ref>

Haisch died on September 3, 2026, at the age of 77, after a several years-long battle with Parkinson's disease.<ref name=“Obituary”>{{Cite web|url=https://neptunesociety.com/obituaries/belmont-ca/bernhard-haisch-13026193|title=Bernhard Haisch |website=Neptune Cremation Service}}</ref>

== Research ==
Haisch published over 130 scientific papers.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.calphysics.org/haisch/|title=Bernard Haisch Curriculum Vitae|publisher=Calphysics Institute|access-date=2025-10-18}}</ref> He served as a scientific editor of the ''[[The Astrophysical Journal|Astrophysical Journal]]'' from 1993 to 2002,<ref name="Beyond" /> and editor-in-chief of the ''[[Journal of Scientific Exploration]]'' from 1988 to 1999.<ref name="Haisch_Sims_2004">{{cite journal|author1=Haisch, Bernard|author2=Sims, Marsha|year=2004|title=A Retrospective on the ''Journal of Scientific Exploration''|journal=Journal of Scientific Exploration|volume=18|issue=1|url=https://www.scientificexploration.org/docs/18/jse_18_1_haisch.pdf|archive-date=2024-05-22|access-date=2024-02-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240522181111/https://www.scientificexploration.org/docs/18/jse_18_1_haisch.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> He has been listed in ''[[American Men & Women of Science]]'' under general physics.<ref name="AMWS" />

In the 1990s, Haisch and Alfonso Rueda developed a "quantum vacuum inertia" hypothesis responsible for mass.<ref name="Matthews_1994">{{cite journal|author=Matthews, Robert|date=February 4, 1994|title=Inertia: Does Empty Space Put Up the Resistance?|journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]]|volume=263|issue=5147|pages=612–613|doi=10.1126/science.263.5147.612 |pmid=17747645 |bibcode=1994Sci...263..612M }}</ref><ref name="Powel_1994">{{cite magazine|author=Powell, Corey S.|date=May 1994|title=Unbearable Lightness|magazine=[[Scientific American]]|volume=270|issue=5|pages=27–28|doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0594-27}}</ref><ref name="Levin_2009">{{cite journal|author=Levin, Yefim S.|date=January 27, 2009|title=Inertia as a zero-point-field force: Critical analysis of the Haisch-Rueda-Puthoff inertia theory|journal=[[Physical Review A]]|volume=79 |issue=1 |article-number=012114 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.79.012114 |bibcode=2009PhRvA..79a2114L |url=https://journals.aps.org/pra/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevA.79.012114}}</ref> The inertialess "SHARP drive" in [[Arthur C. Clarke]]'s ''[[3001: The Final Odyssey]]'' was named for [[Andrei Sakharov]], Haisch, Rueda, and [[Harold E. Puthoff]].<ref name="Clarke_1997">{{cite book|author=Clarke, Arthur C.|authorlink=Arthur C. Clarke|year=1997|title=[[3001: The Final Odyssey]]|pages=64,255–256}}</ref><ref name="Gilster_2004">{{cite book|author=Gilster, Paul|year=2004|title=Centauri Dreams: Imagining and Planning Interstellar Exploration|pages=174}}</ref>

In 2006, he proposed that quantum fields that pervade all of space could give rise to consciousness in systems of sufficient complexity, a view inspired in part by the ideas of physicist [[Roger Penrose]].<ref name="NBC">{{cite web |last=Powell |first=Corey S. |author-link=Corey S. Powell |title=Is the Universe Conscious? |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/mach/ncna772956 |website=NBC News |date=June 16, 2017 |publisher=NBCUniversal News Group |access-date=October 12, 2025}}</ref>

== Theological and philosophical writings ==
Haisch was a [[Catholic]] [[seminarian]] in the past.{{sfnq|Creekmore|2013|q=Haisch, a distinguished scientist and former Catholic seminarian...}} Haisch's writings on science and theology propose that scientific and spiritual worldviews can be reconciled through an understanding of the universe as both physical and conscious. His 2006 book ''The God Theory: Universes, Zero-Point Fields, and What's Behind It All'' presented a model in which consciousness is a fundamental aspect of reality rather than an accidental byproduct of matter.<ref name="Smith">{{cite journal |last=Smith |first=Stephen P. |title=Review of Bernard Haisch's Book: The God Theory: Universes, Zeropoint Fields, and What's Behind It All |journal=Scientific GOD Journal |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=307–309 |date=June 2010 |url=https://scispace.com/pdf/review-of-bernard-haisch-s-book-the-god-theory-universes-1q88ianh3l.pdf |access-date=October 12, 2025}}</ref>  

In the follow-up, ''The Purpose-Guided Universe: Believing in Einstein, Darwin, and God'' (2010), Haisch argues for a synthesis of scientific discovery and spiritual understanding, maintaining that belief in a universal intelligence is compatible with evolutionary and cosmological science.<ref name="Foreword">{{cite web |last=Charpentier |first=Julia Ann |title=The Purpose-Guided Universe: Believing in Einstein, Darwin, and God |url=https://www.forewordreviews.com/reviews/the-purpose-guided-universe/ |website=Foreword Reviews |date=July–August 2010 |publisher=Foreword Magazine, Inc. |access-date=October 12, 2025}}</ref> Reviewer Julia Ann Charpentier described the book as “an enlightening exploration of creation and the human being’s existence on Earth” that bridges the perceived gap between religion and science.<ref name="Foreword" />

Haisch's works often explored ideas related to [[panpsychism]] and the fine-tuning of physical constants, engaging with debates about the role of consciousness in the cosmos and the philosophical implications of quantum physics.<ref name="NBC" /><ref name="Smith" />
